reviewRows.title: Persistent kidney-allograft dysfunction: investigation
fairness: Biopsy is the best listed cause-defining investigation for persistent dysfunction after the represented volume and structural assessment. Missed doses raise suspicion without establishing rejection. Plasma BK testing is useful concurrently but does not replace tissue classification; scintigraphy has less incremental value here.

Two consequential steps remain: interpret why the initial assessment does not explain the sustained dysfunction, then select the investigation that distinguishes parenchymal causes. This is a core transplant workup decision.

The negative structural findings are necessary clinical boundaries, not a reliable nonmedical wording shortcut. Options are parallel investigations; no unique length, absolute, teaching sentence or key-only task phrase selects the answer.

First node is self-contained. Its explanation appropriately stops before naming the next node's treatment. A target-range tacrolimus result does not exclude every form of calcineurin-inhibitor injury; the explanation is appropriately limited to excessive measured exposure.

Scope of this report: all 23 proposed executable nodes (20 new and 3 rewritten) were reviewed against their candidate visible fields. The 3 kept records, including 2 parked drafts, 29 retired/replacement input records and other held/unkeyed records are noted but not re-reviewed. No standalone exhibit is present in these candidate nodes. PASS is editorial, not clinical approval; all drafts still require Melissa Rowland's exact-version sign-off. This offline review did not verify sources, runtime waits or rendering, and highYield is qualitative general-surgery relevance, not measured examination frequency.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between a prioritized tissue investigation and concurrent viral testing; do not teach that BK testing is unnecessary in graft dysfunction.

reviewRows.title: Initial treatment of a cellular graft-injury pattern
clarityIssues: The biopsy describes interstitial inflammation and tubulitis but does not state whether arteries were represented or whether intimal arteritis/aggressive vascular injury was present. Absence of microvascular inflammation is not the same information.
When selected independently, this node lacks the prior node's ongoing graft dysfunction; the generic presentation only says an outside transplant admission is being reviewed.
fairness: Methylprednisolone is a defensible initial treatment for the intended nonaggressive cellular process. However, the steroid-versus-ATG distinction depends partly on severity/vascular findings that the visible record does not supply. Do not infer their absence from omitted findings. This is an underspecification concern, not a claim that the proposed drug is clinically wrong.

Interpreting the tissue/infection findings and then choosing initial rather than rescue therapy are two consequential steps. The competing therapies are real and similarly phrased; necessary BK and humoral studies should not be deleted to manufacture difficulty.
The sequence follows the biopsy node coherently and its earlier explanation does not disclose methylprednisolone. The central concept is high yield.
suggestions: Provide a source-supported biopsy description that establishes the intended cellular severity and arterial assessment; do not invent a Banff grade or threshold.
Briefly retain the persistent graft dysfunction in this node's update so the treatment indication survives independent selection.
Have the clinician confirm the steroid-versus-ATG ranking against the completed biopsy description.

reviewRows.title: Persistent cellular rejection after steroid treatment
fairness: Rabbit ATG is the best listed escalation given continued dysfunction after a completed steroid course, repeat active interstitial/tubular lymphocytic injury and contemporaneous exclusion of the represented viral/humoral alternatives. The wording 'consider' appropriately avoids a universal rescue prescription.

Two decisions are consequential: establish that the persistent injury remains cellular rather than infer its mechanism from steroid failure, then select lymphocyte depletion at the rescue stage. Plasma exchange/IVIG and maintenance reduction are meaningful mechanism errors.

This is a separate single-node case and includes the prior treatment and repeat tissue record needed to stand alone. It does not require seeing the earlier steroid question. No reliable nonmedical cue selects ATG, although the summarized humoral exclusion makes the item moderate rather than hard.
suggestions: Preserve the repeat-biopsy and treatment-response evidence; do not shorten this into 'steroids failed, choose ATG.'

reviewRows.title: Isolated BK viruria and maintenance treatment
fairness: Maintaining the regimen with repeat plasma assessment is the best listed plan for the supplied isolated urinary detection, negative contemporaneous plasma result and stable graft function. The wording does not invent a treatment threshold or monitoring interval.

The resident must distinguish the significance of the specimen compartments, then decide whether the finding justifies the consequential risk of reducing immunosuppression. Immediate reduction is a credible error; leflunomide is a weaker but recognizable treatment misconception.

Shared repeat-plasma wording appears in every option, so it does not select the key. 'Maintenance' in the task applies to all three plans. The negative plasma result is decision-critical evidence requiring medical interpretation, not a vocabulary giveaway.

This first node is self-contained. Its explanation distinguishes viruria from DNAemia/nephropathy without explicitly giving the later biopsy-proven treatment answer. The infection-versus-rejection balance is high yield.

reviewRows.title: Biopsy-supported BK nephropathy: treatment direction
fairness: Supervised stepwise maintenance reduction is the best listed direction for the combined plasma/tissue findings in the explicitly low-risk setting without a separate rejection component. Steroid escalation reverses that direction; adding cidofovir is not an equally supported routine alternative.

The resident interprets the tissue and viral trajectory, then balances infection control against graft rejection risk. Low immunologic risk and the absence of concurrent rejection are legitimate boundaries; retaining them is fairer than hiding those treatment-critical conditions.

No option has a reliable nonmedical wording advantage. Increase/reduce/add are parallel treatment directions. The reduction choice is less drug-specific, but does specify the intervention being selected rather than an empty individualized-care slogan.

The later admission is coherent with earlier viruria. The new update supplies the dysfunction, repeated plasma detection and biopsy evidence needed independently. Prior feedback scaffolds the distinction but does not name this treatment. This is high-yield transplant infection management.
suggestions: Keep the low-risk/no-concurrent-rejection boundary attached to this exact version; do not generalize its answer to every BK-positive recipient.

reviewRows.title: Renewed dysfunction after BK improvement
clarityIssues: 'After the represented maintenance reduction' does not identify the preceding BK nephropathy if this later node is selected independently. The presentation itself contains no diagnosis or treatment history.

cues.phrase: The renewed decline has not been sampled.
cues.why: Names an omitted sampling action immediately before the only tissue-sampling choice; it directs a reader to biopsy without interpreting the post-reduction biology.

cues.phrase: adequate graft flow/drainage
cues.why: Together with 'Repeat radionuclide perfusion study', this makes one distractor look like repeating an already settled investigation. Earlier feedback has also explained why urine BK is not the decisive compartment, leaving biopsy by elimination.

fairness: Repeat biopsy is clinically defensible for renewed unexplained dysfunction; no confident clinical error is identified. Undetectable plasma BK does not by itself establish the cause of new graft injury.

The important potential lesson is discordance between virologic improvement and graft function. The current choices let the learner bypass that interpretation through a named omission and two low-value repeat tests, so two consequential steps are not effectively tested.
The three-part chronology is coherent when read together, but prior urine-versus-plasma feedback weakens the final distractor set.
suggestions: Delete the named sampling omission; retain the actual trajectory and necessary structural assessment.
Restate briefly that maintenance immunosuppression was reduced for biopsy-supported BK disease.

Compare plausible responses to discordant graft and viral trajectories, such as tissue reassessment versus a specific empiric immunosuppression change or continued surveillance, with sufficient observations to distinguish them. Re-solve the new choices clinically rather than merely renaming the repeat tests.

reviewRows.title: Tacrolimus interaction and excess exposure

cues.phrase: A verified predose tacrolimus concentration then exceeded the service's target
cues.why: The only option that changes tacrolimus is 'Reduce or temporarily interrupt tacrolimus'. An above-target drug level matched to a reduction of that same drug answers the item without using clarithromycin, the renal findings or tremor.

cues.phrase: Reduce or temporarily interrupt tacrolimus
cues.why: The key uniquely offers a flexible two-action response, while both distractors simply reduce a different drug. This reinforces the direct target-level match.

fairness: The drug interaction, renal dysfunction and tremor support the intended tacrolimus adjustment; addressing the antibiotic interaction concurrently is correctly represented. No unsupported dose is given.

This is high-yield pharmacology, but the tested operation is currently matching an excessive concentration to its drug. The other maintenance drugs are not credible competing targets for this exposure problem.
The node stands alone and the later stable visit is plausible. Its explanation explicitly teaches a verified predose/trough boundary that further simplifies the next node.
suggestions: Retain the clinically necessary exposure and symptom evidence, but change the decision so the interaction or response trajectory affects the plan rather than merely identifying the named high drug.

Use comparably specific management alternatives that address the same tacrolimus problem and differ in a supported sequencing or interaction-management decision. Avoid invented dose-reduction percentages or holding thresholds.
If retained as a simple medication-safety recognition item, obtain explicit acceptance of that basic role instead of labeling it a difficult two-step resident question.

reviewRows.title: Mislabelled tacrolimus trough collection
clarityIssues: 'Intended tacrolimus monitoring question' is less concrete than naming the actual decision about the reported result and current dose.

cues.phrase: A verified predose tacrolimus concentration
cues.why: The preceding node supplies this collection definition, and its explanation calls the result a 'verified high trough'. The later key, 'Collect tacrolimus immediately before the next dose', repeats the taught definition.

cues.phrase: a specimen labeled tacrolimus trough
cues.why: The options only ask when to draw a trough. Once the definition is known, the administration discrepancy and recovered clinical course are unnecessary to selecting the before-dose choice.

fairness: The keyed predose collection is correct for the intended trough, and the explanation correctly distinguishes a printed test name from actual collection timing.

This is one collection-definition skill rather than two consequential decisions. The important safety issue is whether to change medication on an invalid high result; the task does not make the learner decide that.
The later visit is coherent and the update is independently understandable, although 'the tremor has resolved' references prior context. The earlier explanation substantially scaffolds the answer.
suggestions: Ask for the next monitoring/medication action, using invalid timing plus recovered graft function to distinguish repeat correctly timed testing from an immediate dose change.
Offer comparable concrete plans, and revise earlier feedback so it does not rehearse the exact scored collection answer.
If the sole objective remains trough timing, seek explicit basic-skill acceptance and label the difficulty honestly.

reviewRows.title: Progressive lymphadenopathy despite falling EBV DNA
fairness: Representative tissue biopsy is the best listed diagnostic priority for progressive nodal disease and an unclassifiable aspirate. Falling blood EBV does not classify the lesion; PET/CT can contribute to staging or target selection but does not replace tissue diagnosis.

The resident must interpret discordant blood and lesion trajectories, then recognize that the previous specimen did not establish a tissue diagnosis. The explicit sample inadequacy is necessary evidence rather than an invented omission cue.
All options are investigations of comparable scope. Staging versus diagnosis is a real clinical distinction here, not a grammatical task mismatch. No strong nonmedical cue uniquely selects biopsy.
This first node is self-contained and its explanation does not give the next immunosuppression answer. PTLD evaluation is high yield; the exact biopsy technique is appropriately outside this task.
suggestions: Remove the learner-facing editorial sentence beginning 'This item selects'; keep the clinical distinction that tissue diagnosis is needed without adding an unsupported technique/handling rule.

reviewRows.title: Immunosuppression after PTLD diagnosis

cues.phrase: The later tissue record establishes polymorphic B-cell PTLD
cues.why: Providing a diagnosis is legitimate in management questions, but here it supplies all interpretation needed for the remaining single association: PTLD leads to reduced immunosuppression. The added staging and graft observations do not create a genuine competing decision.

fairness: Supervised reduction is a defensible initial component of care in this setting. The item does not claim it is the entire oncology regimen, which is appropriate.

Increase/continue/reduce is a direction-only option set; increasing CNI exposure has little credibility after explicit PTLD, stable graft function and no rejection. The neutral phrasing does not turn this into difficult two-step reasoning.

The later biopsy coherently follows the tissue-investigation node and is self-contained. Prior feedback does not directly disclose the answer. The underlying PTLD/immunosuppression principle is high yield.
suggestions: Retain the diagnosis if the objective is management, but introduce a source-supported competing graft or disease-course consideration that actually changes the initial plan, with specific same-stage alternatives.
Do not expand into the held CD20 escalation question without separate evidence and authorization. If this remains a foundation-level direction question, request explicit basic-role acceptance.

reviewRows.title: Persistent transplant diarrhea with negative plasma CMV
fairness: Ileocolonoscopy with mucosal biopsy best distinguishes the represented mucosal causes, including CMV disease and mycophenolate-related injury. Repeated negative plasma testing does not exclude localized gastrointestinal CMV; an immunity assay does not establish the cause of colitis.

Two steps remain: recognize the limits of a negative blood result in this clinical setting, then choose a test that can assess the organ process and its competing cause. Mycophenolate is a useful alternative explanation rather than decorative medication history.

The negative plasma results weaken the repeat-plasma option, but they are indispensable to the tested misconception, and the immune-assay alternative still requires medical understanding. No unique wording, length, absolute or diagnostic label supplies the answer.

The first node is self-contained. The subsequent tissue result and treatment questions follow coherently; this explanation does not name the later antiviral route. The concept is relevant to common transplant infection testing.

reviewRows.title: Initial antiviral route for gastrointestinal CMV

cues.phrase: prevented reliable oral medication intake
cues.why: Supplies the route interpretation before the decision, eliminating the oral option by ordinary language. The remaining choice is basic initial-drug recall, not an independently inferred severity/absorption decision.

cues.phrase: Oral valganciclovir with renal dose adjustment
cues.why: Paired with 'Intravenous ganciclovir with renal dose adjustment', the similar drug names suggest a route pair, while foscarnet is the naming outlier. This is a weaker lexical hint, but combined with the explicit oral-route exclusion it further simplifies the set.

fairness: Intravenous ganciclovir with renal adjustment is the defensible listed initial plan for the supplied tissue diagnosis and inability to take reliable oral treatment. Foscarnet has no represented resistance or intolerance indication. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.
The diagnosis is legitimately established for a management task, but the route conclusion is also supplied; the current item tests a familiar first-line drug association with a preselected route.
The tissue result coherently follows the earlier investigation. The update and common presentation provide enough context for independent selection. The antiviral principle is high yield.
suggestions: Retain actual vomiting/intake observations needed for a fair route decision, while removing the authored conclusion about reliable oral exposure.

Make the drug decision consequential through a supported competing toxicity, prior-treatment or response consideration and clinically credible same-stage alternatives. A wording-only replacement of the oral-intake sentence will not by itself create difficulty.
If retained as initial-treatment recognition, explicitly accept that easier educational purpose.

reviewRows.title: Leukopenia during active CMV treatment
clarityIssues: 'White-cell counts fall' does not establish the degree or clinical significance of leukopenia/neutropenia. A falling count can remain normal; the reader cannot tell how strongly a medication change is indicated.
'Adjust mycophenolate' does not say reduce, hold or otherwise change it, while the competing options prescribe explicit changes.

cues.phrase: Adjust mycophenolate and retain valganciclovir
cues.why: The key alone uses an unspecified flexible adjustment. It is easier to defend than the specific antiviral reductions/substitution offered as alternatives, creating an individualized-answer advantage.

fairness: The intended principle is defensible: do not underdose an appropriately renal-adjusted antiviral during required CMV treatment merely because of leukopenia; address other marrow-suppressive therapy and count support. Letermovir is not an interchangeable routine treatment substitute in this scenario.

It remains uncertain from the visible count description whether mycophenolate modification is required now rather than monitoring/support while preserving both drugs. This is missing decision-critical information, not a claim that the intended management direction is wrong.

There are potentially two consequential steps: interpret the cytopenia in the context of renal dosing and ongoing antiviral need, then choose which treatment to modify. The later course is coherent and sufficiently summarizes the prior CMV treatment to stand alone.
suggestions: Supply a clinician-reviewed description or supported values showing clinically meaningful cytopenia, including the relevant neutrophil information if it drives action. Do not invent a treatment threshold.
Specify the intended mycophenolate action at the same level of precision as the alternatives and confirm that it is uniquely appropriate under the supplied graft/rejection-risk context.
Preserve the verified renal dose and ongoing treatment indication; they are necessary to distinguishing a justified renal adjustment from inappropriate antiviral underexposure.

reviewRows.title: Compatibility testing after a sensitizing event
clarityIssues: 'Changed compatibility assessment' is an abstract task description; the concrete issue is whether the recipient's current antibody status is represented by the stored specimen.

cues.phrase: The donor's ABO and HLA typing were completed and have not changed.
cues.why: Explicitly dismisses both donor-retesting distractors. The key is the only recipient test; a reader can match the changed recipient to that option without knowing sensitization biology.

cues.phrase: archived specimen collected before that transfusion
cues.why: Repeats the same before/after contrast already supplied in the opening sentence. Combined with the unchanged-donor sentence, it leaves an obvious update-the-recipient answer.

fairness: Updated recipient HLA-antibody characterization is defensible after the represented transfusion. The explanation correctly avoids specifying an unsupported sampling interval.

The principle is high yield, but repeating stable donor genotype/blood group is not a credible near-miss. The current node is a single sensitization association with explicit elimination of both competitors.
This first node stands alone and provides a coherent transition to the subsequent donor-antigen comparison.
suggestions: Remove the sentence declaring both donor alternatives unchanged and replace the option set with plausible recipient compatibility investigations or specimen-use plans.
Make the sensitizing-event chronology determine which current evidence is needed; state enough laboratory context to avoid ranking equally indicated tests without a reason.
Do not invent a post-transfusion testing interval to manufacture a second step.

reviewRows.title: Donor antigen matching against recipient antibodies
clarityIssues: 'Least represented donor-specific antibody concern' is awkward wording that obscures a simple comparison. It is appropriately bounded, but could state the exact compatibility question more naturally.

cues.phrase: recipient antibodies directed to HLA-A2 and HLA-B7
cues.why: The key, 'His friend: HLA-A11 and HLA-B44', is the only option with neither printed target. Literal symbol matching solves the item without medical knowledge or interpreting a clinical consequence.

fairness: The friend is the uniquely defensible answer to the narrowly limited represented-antigen question. The disclaimer about further crossmatch work appropriately prevents claiming complete compatibility or authorization to transplant.

The antigen components themselves are balanced across the four options; this is not a majority-component convergence problem. The problem is that avoidance of two supplied labels is the whole scored operation.

The current antibody profile makes the second node self-contained and the prior sensitization node follows coherently. Kinship is incidental because no actual relationship-dependent tradeoff must be resolved.
Donor-specific antibodies versus donor relationship is a high-yield principle, but this implementation is a one-step matching exercise.
suggestions: Either explicitly accept a foundational antigen-matching exercise or redesign around a source-supported compatibility decision in which interpreting the antibody/antigen result changes the next action.
Use concrete parallel workup decisions and retain the boundary that this limited panel does not establish overall compatibility. Avoid inventing antibody strength or crossmatch thresholds.

reviewRows.title: Elective mTOR conversion with an open incision

cues.phrase: Replace tacrolimus with sirolimus for maintenance
cues.why: Together with 'Replace tacrolimus with everolimus for maintenance', this creates two similarly worded conversion options and one continuation outlier. Both alternatives share the same clinically relevant class problem; a single mTOR-wound fact eliminates both.

fairness: Deferring an elective mTOR conversion is defensible with an open surgical wound and tolerable tremor. No confident inaccuracy is identified.

The mild symptom and stable graft largely remove the competing reason to change tacrolimus. Distinguishing sirolimus from everolimus does not matter to the tested wound concern, so there is no genuine second decision.

The standalone node is complete and the wound observation is necessary clinical information. mTOR-associated wound-healing concerns are high yield; the present distractor pair makes the application easy.
suggestions: Replace one interchangeable mTOR distractor with a distinct, clinically credible same-stage regimen plan.

Require interpretation of a supported competing CNI adverse-effect or recovery consideration that changes whether/how conversion should proceed. Preserve wound status rather than hiding the contraindicating observation.
Do not create exact timing or dose rules without support; alternatively seek acceptance as an easy safety-recognition item.

reviewRows.title: Preconception antimetabolite selection

cues.phrase: reviewing fetal medication risks
cues.why: The only option that removes the current antimetabolite is 'Replace mycophenolate with azathioprine'; the other two merely retain it at the same or lower dose. The explicit risk framing and unique replacement choice support an answer shortcut.

fairness: Substitution of mycophenolate with a pregnancy-compatible alternative under the transplant team is the defensible direction among these choices. The explanation correctly rejects the assumption that a lower mycophenolate dose establishes fetal safety.
The visible context does not require a second inference beyond the familiar mycophenolate-pregnancy association. Stable graft function and specialist involvement do not create a competing plan.
The node is self-contained and the later azathioprine interaction follows coherently. This is a high-yield adverse-effect concept; no exact transition interval should be inferred from this draft.
suggestions: Move generic fetal-risk teaching out of the vignette unless it describes an essential patient goal, and make any additional patient information affect the medication decision.
Use a supported competing graft/stability or transition-sequencing issue with realistic alternatives, rather than two degrees of continuing the same teratogenic drug.
If the intended purpose is basic preconception medication recognition, seek explicit acceptance of that role instead of calling it two-step.

reviewRows.title: Azathioprine interaction and a misleading gout substitute
fairness: Stopping allopurinol is the best listed additional change in the represented cytopenic interaction. Substituting febuxostat does not resolve the relevant xanthine-oxidase interaction, and unchanged tacrolimus exposure/renal function does not support tacrolimus reduction as the solution.

Two consequential steps remain: attribute the new marrow findings to the azathioprine/allopurinol combination, then reject a superficially plausible gout-drug substitution that shares the interaction. The exposure chronology is necessary evidence, not a sufficient nonmedical route to excluding febuxostat.

The service is already addressing cytopenias and assessing azathioprine, so the question is reasonably limited to an additional medication change rather than a complete marrow-suppression treatment plan. No dose correction is asserted.
The node explicitly restates the current regimen and deferred pregnancy attempts, so it stands alone and coherently follows the substitution node. This is high-yield drug-interaction knowledge.
suggestions: Explain after answering why febuxostat is also unsuitable with azathioprine; this is the most valuable close-distractor lesson and is missing from the main explanation.

Clarify that stopping allopurinol is the selected additional action while azathioprine/cytopenia management continues. Replace 'This question does not choose between those strategies' with a clinical statement that does not appear to disown the action just selected.

reviewRows.title: Immediate graft injury and preformed antibody evidence
clarityIssues: 'Focused event review' asks for an abstract review theme rather than a defined clinical or laboratory decision. 'Review cellular rejection control' is particularly vague.
The cell type and assay underlying 'reacted with donor cells' are unspecified, which becomes consequential when the following node reports a negative HLA antibody/cell-binding evaluation.

cues.phrase: Archived recipient serum drawn before implantation reacted with donor cells
cues.why: The key 'Review preimplantation antibody compatibility' echoes the sample timing and immune-reactivity description. Selecting a review label adds no distinct action after recognizing the supplied classic pattern.

fairness: The combined immediate injury, endothelial immune deposits, microvascular thrombi and pre-event donor reactivity support the intended preformed-antibody concern; the explanation appropriately avoids claiming exclusive causation.

However, mechanism recognition followed by a synonymous review category is one classification, not two consequential steps. The core hyperacute-rejection concept is high yield, but the action is insufficiently concrete.

This node is answerable independently. Across the pair, the earlier positive donor-cell result and later negative HLA/cell-binding record are potentially confusing. Different targets or methods could reconcile them; the text does not identify such a distinction, so this review does not declare the laboratory results impossible.
suggestions: Ask a concrete supported event-investigation decision rather than a broad review theme, with alternatives representing plausible errors at that same stage.
Clarify the target and timing of the donor-cell reaction enough to distinguish it from the next node's HLA assessment, or revise the case chronology so the findings are explicitly compatible.
Preserve the control result and microvascular evidence; do not make timing alone establish the mechanism.

reviewRows.title: ABO pathway and pretreatment compatibility evidence
clarityIssues: 'Reconcile ABO records using preimplantation serum' does not specify what clinical question the archive review will answer or what is being assessed in that serum. Records reconciliation is too broad to make the proposed action concrete.

The current negative 'HLA antibody/cell-binding evaluation' appears inconsistent with the prior donor-cell reaction unless different cells, methods or targets are intended. That distinction is not visible.
When selected independently, 'for the event' has no description of the graft event beyond the generic presentation; the reason to reconstruct pretreatment compatibility is underexplained.
fairness: The intended two decisions are meaningful: distinguish the ABO pathway from HLA testing, then choose evidence obtained before plasma exchange to assess the pre-event state. A negative HLA evaluation does not resolve ABO compatibility.

The four combinations balance ABO/HLA and pre/post-treatment components, so majority-component convergence does not select the key. The sample timing is necessary evidence rather than a prohibited hint.

The intended ABO/preimplantation answer is defensible at the broad level asked, but uniqueness of a specific archive plan cannot be fully assessed while 'reconcile' remains undefined. No assertion that all ABO-incompatible transplantation is prohibited is made.

ABO versus HLA compatibility is high yield. This particular archive formulation is less directly testable than a concrete interpretation or action, and the paired-record ambiguity requires repair before passing.
suggestions: State the event and the precise question being answered about the pre-treatment ABO pathway, with concrete parallel archive/interpretation plans.
Reconcile the earlier positive donor-cell reaction and current negative HLA/cell-binding result explicitly without inventing assay specificity.
Retain the distinction between pre-event and post-plasma-exchange evidence, but do not expand into held assay/allocation or specimen-handling teaching without supported review.

reviewRows.title: Treatment backbone for active antibody-mediated rejection

cues.phrase: The integrated report identified active antibody-mediated rejection without a cellular component or chronic transplant glomerulopathy.
cues.why: Supplies the mechanism and disease-phase interpretations of all preceding raw findings. It also removes the cellular alternative before the options, leaving a standard named-diagnosis-to-treatment association.

fairness: Plasma exchange/IVIG is the defensible listed consensus backbone for the represented acute active process, with baseline therapy/steroids already addressed. The explanation properly acknowledges weak comparative evidence and does not claim an optimal universal regimen or extrapolate to chronic active AMR.

Naming a diagnosis in a management question is not inherently unfair. Here, however, no additional consequential constraint must be interpreted; ATG and maintenance reduction are mechanism-mismatch foils rather than close management alternatives.
The standalone case is complete. AMR recognition and treatment are high yield, but the current item is basic treatment recall, not difficult two-step reasoning.
suggestions: If the objective includes mechanism interpretation, remove the integrated diagnosis label while retaining supported raw tissue, antibody and chronicity findings needed for a unique classification.

Alternatively retain the diagnosis and test a genuinely distinct, supported care-phase decision with credible same-stage alternatives. Do not imply stronger comparative evidence for a particular regimen than is available.
Reassess difficulty after the repair; merely lengthening the pathology description will not make routine regimen recall hard.

reviewRows.title: Persisting delayed graft function: cause-defining investigation
clarityIssues: 'Through the represented surveillance course' provides no usable clinical chronology. The resident cannot tell whether this is the immediate postoperative course or sufficiently persistent unexplained dysfunction at a later reassessment.

cues.phrase: Serial Doppler studies show patent graft vessels, and urinary drainage is adequate.
cues.why: Against 'Repeat graft Doppler ultrasonography' and 'Perform radionuclide graft scintigraphy', both alternatives revisit structural/perfusion questions already presented as settled. The only new diagnostic modality is biopsy. Necessary normal findings should remain, but this option set makes them an elimination scaffold.

fairness: Biopsy is a reasonable cause-defining investigation during persistent delayed function, and delayed function alone cannot distinguish preservation injury from rejection. No confident clinical inaccuracy in that principle is identified.

The timing/trajectory is too vague to establish how urgently biopsy should be prioritized over continued reassessment. The explanation's qualified 'can warrant biopsy' is less definite than the task's best-next-investigation ranking. This requires clarification rather than an invented universal day threshold.

The first node is independently understandable but largely repeats the earlier persistent-dysfunction biopsy construct. The offered choices do not require a distinct two-step delayed-function inference.
Delayed graft function is high yield and the subsequent recovery node follows coherently.
suggestions: Replace 'represented surveillance course' with a concrete, source-supported clinical chronology and trajectory sufficient to justify the intended reassessment; do not invent a universal postoperative cutoff.
Use credible competing cause-assessment or management plans at the current stage, rather than two already-resolved perfusion investigations.
Make this node test what is distinctive about delayed function or consolidate redundant biopsy-selection coverage while preserving stable concept/history rules.

reviewRows.title: Tacrolimus during recovering delayed graft function
fairness: Continuing the selected tacrolimus regimen is the best listed plan with biopsy-described tubular injury, improving graft function and verified target exposure. Prior dialysis alone is not a sufficient reason to withhold CNI until complete recovery. The explanation correctly calls for reassessment if toxicity or deterioration emerges.

The resident must distinguish recovering delayed function from ongoing drug toxicity/rejection, then weigh continuation against reflex withholding or substitution. Withholding a potentially nephrotoxic CNI is a credible competing error; the response trajectory actually changes that decision.

The options compare concrete CNI plans with similar scope. Improving urine output/creatinine and target exposure are legitimate clinical evidence, not a unique lexical cue. No convergence or explanatory-option shortcut identifies the key.

The biopsy and earlier dialysis history are restated sufficiently for independent selection. The sequence follows the cause-evaluation node coherently, and its prior explanation did not disclose the continuation answer. This is high-yield transplant medication reasoning.
suggestions: In post-answer feedback, briefly explain why immediate sirolimus substitution is not a justified default response to this recovering course, without implying an unseen wound complication or inventing a conversion timeline.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 48-year-old woman, attends clinic to discuss an outside kidney-transplant admission with the founder.

nodes.objective: Choose cause-defining graft evaluation before empiric rejection therapy.
nodes.currentUpdate: The outside record shows a sustained creatinine rise after several missed immunosuppressant doses. Creatinine remains above her prior baseline after volume replacement. Doppler shows flow in the graft artery and vein; ultrasound shows no collecting-system dilation. The correctly timed tacrolimus result is within the team's documented target.
nodes.task: Which investigation should the transplant team prioritize for {patientName}'s persistent graft dysfunction?

choices.label: Plasma BK quantitative nucleic-acid assay
choices.rationale: Useful for infection screening, but cannot classify the competing tissue processes causing established dysfunction.
choices.temptation: Attribute graft dysfunction to a common viral complication.
choices.reasonableWhen: BK screening is due in a recipient with stable graft function.

choices.label: Kidney-allograft core tissue biopsy
choices.rationale: The persistent unexplained dysfunction requires tissue to distinguish rejection, infection and other injury.
choices.temptation: Resolve the cause before selecting antirejection treatment.
choices.reasonableWhen: Persistent unexplained allograft dysfunction with a clinically suitable biopsy.

choices.label: Radionuclide graft perfusion scintigraphy
choices.rationale: Adds functional drainage information but does not characterize the likely parenchymal process after the represented vascular and collecting-system studies.
choices.temptation: Repeat a noninvasive graft test before accepting biopsy risk.
choices.reasonableWhen: An equivocal drainage study leaves obstruction as the main unresolved question.

nodes.explanation: Obstruction, gross vascular failure and excessive measured tacrolimus exposure do not explain this persistent course. Tissue assessment can separate rejection from mimics before the team chooses treatment. The missed doses raise concern but do not establish a tissue diagnosis.

reasoning.interpret: Interpret persistent dysfunction after correction of volume status and adequate initial structural assessment.
reasoning.apply: Choose tissue evaluation rather than infer a rejection mechanism from missed doses.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Sustained dysfunction remains unexplained after represented volume, flow and drainage assessment.
reasoning.counterfactual: If graft function were stable and the task were routine BK surveillance, plasma BK testing would be appropriate.
reasoning.consequence: Empiric immunosuppression escalation can worsen an unrecognized infection.
reasoning.deletionTest: Missed doses create rejection concern; target-level exposure avoids a toxicity assumption. Volume response and adequate Doppler/drainage results delimit the remaining question. No unrelated symptoms retained.
reasoning.cueAttack: The task names no biopsy or missing action. All options are investigations and all receive wait proposals. The key is not the only cautious choice; each test has a distinct diagnostic scope.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three specific investigations during cause determination.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The close error is treating the adherence history as enough to direct therapy or substituting viral screening for tissue classification.
reasoning.sequenceReview: First node. Its feedback names no specific antirejection drug.

repairHistory: Author gate applied to this exact version; the concrete attacks and retained boundaries are recorded in reasoning.

nodes.objective: Choose initial therapy for a biopsy-supported cellular process.
nodes.currentUpdate: The returned biopsy shows mononuclear interstitial infiltration with cells crossing tubular epithelium. Polyomavirus staining and plasma BK testing are negative. There is no microvascular inflammation or endothelial C4d staining, and donor-specific HLA antibodies are not detected. The team has not yet given antirejection treatment.
nodes.task: Which initial antirejection treatment best fits {patientName}'s returned graft findings?

choices.label: Intravenous antithymocyte globulin therapy
choices.rationale: Lymphocyte depletion is an escalation option for resistant or aggressive cellular rejection; that stage is not represented.
choices.temptation: Choose a stronger T-cell treatment whenever tubules are infiltrated.
choices.reasonableWhen: Cellular rejection persists after appropriate steroid treatment or has aggressive vascular features.

choices.label: Intravenous methylprednisolone pulse therapy
choices.rationale: The findings favor a cellular process, for which corticosteroids are initial treatment.
choices.temptation: Interpret the tissue and then choose the treatment stage.
choices.reasonableWhen: An initial episode of acute cellular rejection without the represented refractory or aggressive vascular course.

choices.label: Plasma exchange with intravenous immunoglobulin therapy
choices.rationale: This targets an antibody-mediated pathway; the represented tissue and serology favor a cellular process.
choices.temptation: Treat any rejection as antibody removal.
choices.reasonableWhen: Acute active antibody-mediated rejection is established by the full tissue and antibody assessment.

nodes.explanation: The tissue and infection studies support an initial cellular-rejection pathway. Start with corticosteroid treatment under the transplant team; reserve lymphocyte depletion for an appropriate refractory or aggressive course.

reasoning.interpret: Interpret the tubular/interstitial pattern together with viral, microvascular and antibody studies.
reasoning.apply: Apply the initial-treatment stage rather than jump to cellular rescue or an antibody-focused regimen.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The cellular pattern is present before any represented antirejection course and lacks aggressive vascular findings.
reasoning.counterfactual: If repeat tissue showed ongoing cellular rejection after an adequate steroid course, lymphocyte-depleting therapy would become reasonable.
reasoning.consequence: Overtreatment adds infection risk; antibody-directed treatment may miss the dominant cellular process.
reasoning.deletionTest: Tissue distribution earns the mechanism inference. Viral studies preserve a crucial BK boundary. Treatment chronology distinguishes steroids from rescue.
reasoning.cueAttack: No rejection diagnosis is supplied in the update. Necessary negative viral and humoral studies remain because therapies overlap otherwise. All choices are named treatment courses of similar scope.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three antirejection treatment approaches at the initial treatment stage.
reasoning.difficultyReason: Steroids, ATG and PLEX/IVIG are real transplant therapies; tissue mechanism and treatment stage both matter.
reasoning.sequenceReview: Prior feedback only called for biopsy. This update supplies new tissue evidence and does not name the selected drug.

repairHistory: Author gate applied to this exact version; the concrete attacks and retained boundaries are recorded in reasoning.
Used full named treatment courses with parallel scope to repair the short-key word-count outlier. No dose or treatment duration was added.

Second option attack found generic IV/therapy convergence. Made IV treatment scope explicit across all three actual therapies, without changing drugs, doses or stages; re-solved the cellular versus humoral and initial versus rescue comparison.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 48-year-old woman, attends clinic for the founder to examine an outside kidney-transplant treatment-response record.

nodes.objective: Recognize a refractory cellular course before selecting escalation.
nodes.currentUpdate: A later record documents completion of the transplant service's steroid treatment and continued graft deterioration. Repeat biopsy again shows active interstitial and tubular lymphocytic injury. Tissue viral studies remain negative; the contemporaneous antibody and microvascular assessment does not support an antibody-mediated component.
nodes.task: Which escalation should the transplant team consider for {patientName}'s persistent biopsy-supported process?

choices.label: Rabbit antithymocyte globulin
choices.rationale: Persistent cellular injury after the completed steroid course supports consideration of lymphocyte depletion.
choices.temptation: Use actual treatment response and repeat tissue to establish the rescue stage.
choices.reasonableWhen: A refractory cellular episode after reassessment excludes a dominant alternative.

choices.label: Plasma exchange with IVIG
choices.rationale: A stronger treatment is not automatically the correct mechanism; no antibody-mediated component is represented.
choices.temptation: Equate failure of steroids with an antibody mechanism.
choices.reasonableWhen: New antibody-mediated findings emerge on the reassessment.

choices.label: Reduction of maintenance mycophenolate
choices.rationale: This is a BK-directed adjustment, not treatment of the represented persistent cellular injury.
choices.temptation: Avoid further immunosuppression after any failed course.
choices.reasonableWhen: Biopsy instead establishes BK nephropathy without concomitant rejection.

nodes.explanation: A failed steroid course does not by itself identify the next drug. The repeat tissue and contemporaneous studies keep the refractory cellular pathway supported, where lymphocyte depletion can be considered. This is not a universal rescue prescription.

reasoning.interpret: Interpret both the unsuccessful treatment trajectory and the repeated tissue pattern.
reasoning.apply: Select mechanism-directed rescue instead of treating failure itself as a new diagnosis.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The repeat biopsy still supports cellular injury rather than a newly represented humoral or viral cause.
reasoning.counterfactual: If repeat tissue and DSA instead established active AMR, PLEX/IVIG would be a reasonable treatment backbone.
reasoning.consequence: The wrong escalation may compound infection risk without addressing the cause.
reasoning.deletionTest: The repeat biopsy is decisive: deleting it would leave several mechanisms for failed therapy. Completion of the steroid course establishes stage without inventing a duration.
reasoning.cueAttack: Removed a proposed task phrase calling the episode steroid-resistant. The resident must infer that status from response plus tissue. The earlier explanation does not list rescue drug names.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three named immunosuppression interventions at the escalation stage.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The tempting error is changing mechanism because the first treatment failed, despite repeat evidence.
reasoning.sequenceReview: Standalone follow-up with the completed course and repeat biopsy supplied in this encounter. It is not obligatorily chained after the steroid node, whose choice feedback can teach the ATG rescue association. Manager should avoid immediate replay as a difficulty claim.

repairHistory: Author gate applied to this exact version; the concrete attacks and retained boundaries are recorded in reasoning.

Separated from the preceding steroid question because its ATG distractor feedback could rehearse the rescue answer. Current standalone context supplies the necessary course and tissue evidence independently.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old man, comes to clinic with sequential outside kidney-transplant follow-up records for the founder to examine.

nodes.objective: Separate urinary BK detection from disease requiring immunosuppression reduction.
nodes.currentUpdate: Urine testing newly detects BK DNA. Graft function remains at his prior baseline. Plasma BK quantitative testing from the same evaluation does not detect viral DNA. He has no prior biopsy-proven BK disease and remains on his established maintenance regimen.
nodes.task: Which maintenance plan best fits {patientName}'s current BK results?

choices.label: Reduce mycophenolate and repeat plasma BK testing
choices.rationale: Reduction is appropriate for sustained plasma DNAemia or tissue disease, but urine detection with stable function and negative plasma does not establish that stage.
choices.temptation: Treat any positive BK specimen as nephropathy.
choices.reasonableWhen: Subsequent plasma testing or tissue establishes the indication for reduction.

choices.label: Maintain the regimen and repeat plasma BK testing
choices.rationale: The specimen distinction supports continued plasma surveillance rather than an immediate reduction based on urine detection.
choices.temptation: Use the compartment and graft course to select the care stage.
choices.reasonableWhen: Urinary replication is represented without plasma DNAemia or graft dysfunction.

choices.label: Add leflunomide and repeat plasma BK testing
choices.rationale: Leflunomide is not a recommended routine BK strategy and the record has not established plasma or tissue disease.
choices.temptation: Apply an antiviral-sounding treatment to a newly positive urine assay.
choices.reasonableWhen: Not a supported routine choice under current consensus; experimental use would require separate specialist/trial context.

nodes.explanation: Urinary replication is not the same finding as plasma DNAemia or nephropathy. Follow plasma results and graft function; the current record does not support immediate maintenance reduction.

reasoning.interpret: Distinguish the positive urine compartment from the negative plasma result and stable graft course.
reasoning.apply: Choose surveillance at the present disease stage rather than treat all positive viral tests alike.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Plasma remains negative and graft function remains at baseline.
reasoning.counterfactual: If plasma DNAemia became sustained or tissue established BK nephropathy, supervised immunosuppression reduction would be appropriate.
reasoning.consequence: Premature reduction exposes the graft to rejection without the represented treatment indication.
reasoning.deletionTest: The two compartments and stable graft function are necessary. No viral count, universal repeat interval or screening schedule is invented.
reasoning.cueAttack: Both leading plans include the same surveillance. Removed an earlier phrase calling the result isolated viruria because that supplied the interpretation. Leflunomide is a genuine historical temptation but a weaker distractor under current guidance; independent review should judge it.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three maintenance strategies with a shared surveillance component.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The close decision is whether a urine result has reached the plasma/tissue treatment boundary.
reasoning.sequenceReview: First node. No future disease results or treatment strategy are visible.

repairHistory: Author gate applied to this exact version; the concrete attacks and retained boundaries are recorded in reasoning.

nodes.objective: Choose the direction of immunosuppression change for biopsy-proven BK disease.
nodes.currentUpdate: At a later admission creatinine rises and plasma BK DNA remains detectable on repeated specimens. The biopsy shows tubular epithelial nuclear inclusions and positive polyomavirus large-T-antigen staining. The contemporaneous pathology and antibody assessment identifies no separate rejection component; the service records low immunologic risk.
nodes.task: Which treatment direction best fits {patientName}'s later graft findings?

choices.label: Increase immunosuppression with methylprednisolone
choices.rationale: Tubular inflammation can accompany infection. The viral tissue evidence favors reduction rather than steroid escalation.
choices.temptation: Read tubulitis as rejection without integrating viral staining.
choices.reasonableWhen: The tissue instead supports cellular rejection with no active viral process.

choices.label: Reduce maintenance immunosuppression stepwise
choices.rationale: Biopsy-supported BK disease without represented concurrent rejection favors supervised maintenance reduction.
choices.temptation: Combine tissue virology with immunologic risk before selecting direction.
choices.reasonableWhen: Biopsy-proven BK nephropathy without concurrent rejection or high immunologic risk.

choices.label: Add cidofovir to maintenance immunosuppression
choices.rationale: Cidofovir is not recommended routine BK treatment; maintaining the same net immunosuppression misses the principal strategy.
choices.temptation: Prefer direct antiviral treatment over changing graft-protective medication.
choices.reasonableWhen: No routine correct circumstance is established by the retrieved guideline; trial use would be a separate decision.

nodes.explanation: The combined tissue and plasma findings support BK nephropathy. In this represented low-risk setting without concurrent rejection, the main treatment is supervised reduction of maintenance immunosuppression.

reasoning.interpret: Interpret the tubular viral changes with plasma BK, rather than equating all graft inflammation with rejection.
reasoning.apply: Use the absence of a represented concurrent rejection component and low immunologic risk to select reduction.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Viral changes and large-T-antigen staining accompany BK plasma replication.
reasoning.counterfactual: If viral studies were negative and the integrated biopsy supported acute cellular rejection, corticosteroids would become appropriate.
reasoning.consequence: Wrong-direction immunosuppression can worsen viral injury.
reasoning.deletionTest: Tissue viral evidence is essential. Low risk and the contemporaneous rejection assessment delimit where the reduction recommendation applies; no exact drug taper is authored.
reasoning.cueAttack: The prior explanation does not teach a reduction regimen. All choices are specific active interventions. Replaced a generic team-consult key with an actual therapeutic direction.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three treatments at the same disease-treatment stage.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The resident must resist the familiar rejection interpretation of graft dysfunction and tubulitis.
reasoning.sequenceReview: New biopsy earns the decision. Earlier feedback distinguishes specimen compartments without naming the later treatment key.

repairHistory: Author gate applied to this exact version; the concrete attacks and retained boundaries are recorded in reasoning.

nodes.objective: Investigate renewed graft deterioration after a virologic response.
nodes.currentUpdate: After the represented maintenance reduction, serial plasma BK results become undetectable. Creatinine initially improves, then rises again despite unchanged volume status and adequate graft flow/drainage. The tacrolimus predose concentration is within the service's target. The renewed decline has not been sampled.
nodes.task: Which investigation best addresses {patientName}'s renewed graft deterioration?

choices.label: Repeat urine BK quantitative testing
choices.rationale: Urinary detection cannot distinguish the causes of renewed parenchymal dysfunction.
choices.temptation: Assume any recurrence must be visible first in the urine.
choices.reasonableWhen: The task concerns surveillance when function is stable rather than an unexplained new decline.

choices.label: Repeat kidney-allograft biopsy
choices.rationale: Viral response does not establish the cause of a new creatinine rise after reduced immunosuppression. Tissue can address rejection and residual injury.
choices.temptation: Reconcile discordant virologic and functional trajectories before changing treatment.
choices.reasonableWhen: New unexplained graft dysfunction after treatment response.

choices.label: Repeat radionuclide perfusion study
choices.rationale: A further functional perfusion study does not classify parenchymal injury after the adequate represented structural assessment.
choices.temptation: Keep pursuing the previously excluded mechanical pathway.
choices.reasonableWhen: A new equivocal perfusion or drainage finding becomes the leading uncertainty.

nodes.explanation: A negative plasma trend does not classify new graft injury. The post-reduction course raises competing possibilities that require reassessment; do not infer either rejection or persistent BK from the creatinine trend itself.

reasoning.interpret: Recognize that virologic clearance and renal recovery have diverged after lower immunosuppression.
reasoning.apply: Obtain cause-defining tissue rather than automatically reverse or intensify the prior plan.
reasoning.decidingObservation: A new unexplained functional decline follows initial improvement despite plasma clearance.
reasoning.counterfactual: If creatinine remained stable and only surveillance were due, repeat plasma assessment rather than biopsy could be appropriate; with an equivocal new drainage finding, the perfusion/drainage study could become useful.
reasoning.consequence: Guessing the mechanism may worsen either rejection or infection.
reasoning.deletionTest: The initial improvement then renewed decline earns a new question. Patent flow, drainage, volume status and valid trough exclude unresolved first-line mimics without diagnosing rejection.
reasoning.cueAttack: Task does not announce immune reconstitution or rejection. All offered choices are investigations, all have waits, and no numeric viral cutoff is used.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three graft investigations during renewed cause determination.
reasoning.difficultyReason: A prior successful strategy creates anchoring pressure; the learner must avoid treating viral and functional responses as interchangeable.
reasoning.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback names reduction for proven BK but does not name the cause of this later decline. The new chronology changes the required workup.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 50-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside kidney-transplant medication review. The founder reviews drug administration and laboratory collection records.

nodes.objective: Identify an exposure-related graft injury requiring tacrolimus adjustment.
nodes.currentUpdate: During the outside admission clarithromycin was added to tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. A verified predose tacrolimus concentration then exceeded the service's target, while creatinine rose and a new hand tremor appeared. Graft flow and collecting-system studies were unchanged. The antibiotic plan is being revised by the treating service.
nodes.task: Which immunosuppressant adjustment best fits {patientName}'s represented medication course?

choices.label: Reduce mycophenolate exposure
choices.rationale: This does not address the measured tacrolimus excess and the temporal renal/neurological findings.
choices.temptation: Attribute adverse effects to the antimetabolite in a multi-drug regimen.
choices.reasonableWhen: Mycophenolate-related marrow or gastrointestinal toxicity is the represented problem.

choices.label: Reduce or temporarily interrupt tacrolimus
choices.rationale: The interaction and verified excess exposure with compatible toxicity support a transplant-directed tacrolimus adjustment.
choices.temptation: Integrate the added drug, sampling validity and two toxicity domains.
choices.reasonableWhen: Measured excessive trough exposure accompanies compatible toxicity.

choices.label: Reduce maintenance prednisone exposure
choices.rationale: Reducing prednisone does not remove the excessive tacrolimus exposure.
choices.temptation: Focus on steroid adverse effects whenever a transplant regimen causes symptoms.
choices.reasonableWhen: A steroid-related complication is established and graft risk permits a supervised reduction.

nodes.explanation: Clarithromycin can increase tacrolimus exposure. The verified high trough with new renal dysfunction and tremor supports tacrolimus toxicity and a supervised reduction or temporary interruption while the interaction is addressed.

reasoning.interpret: Interpret the new interaction, valid predose result and renal/neurological changes as concordant excess exposure.
reasoning.apply: Adjust the implicated maintenance agent rather than a different immunosuppressant.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The concentration is a valid trough, and the compatible changes follow clarithromycin initiation.
reasoning.counterfactual: If tacrolimus exposure were appropriate and leukopenia followed mycophenolate, adjustment of mycophenolate would become reasonable.
reasoning.consequence: Adjusting the wrong agent leaves toxicity while reducing other graft protection.
reasoning.deletionTest: The antibiotic, true trough, creatinine and tremor each support causation or assay interpretation. The structural study keeps gross graft obstruction from remaining unresolved.
reasoning.cueAttack: The task does not name toxicity, CYP3A or the preferred drug. All choices change one immunosuppressant; the key retains a clinically necessary reduction/interruption range rather than a fabricated dose.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three medication-adjustment targets.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The close error is attributing all multi-agent toxicity to mycophenolate instead of integrating exposure chronology.
reasoning.sequenceReview: First node. Exact targets and doses remain specialist decisions.

repairHistory: Author gate applied to this exact version; the concrete attacks and retained boundaries are recorded in reasoning.

nodes.objective: Use administration and collection chronology before acting on a reported trough.
nodes.currentUpdate: On a later stable visit, a specimen labeled tacrolimus trough is reported above target. The phlebotomy note records her taking the morning tacrolimus while waiting for the blood draw. Creatinine is at baseline and the tremor has resolved.
nodes.task: Which collection best answers {patientName}'s intended tacrolimus monitoring question?

choices.label: Collect tacrolimus immediately before the next dose
choices.rationale: A predose specimen answers the service's intended trough-monitoring question; the earlier post-dose specimen does not.
choices.temptation: Check collection chronology before accepting the reported assay label.
choices.reasonableWhen: The intended clinical assessment is a standard predose trough.

choices.label: Collect tacrolimus immediately after the next dose
choices.rationale: This reproduces a post-dose window rather than the intended trough.
choices.temptation: Repeat the same collection in the hope that reproducibility fixes the mislabeled window.
choices.reasonableWhen: A separate specified pharmacokinetic protocol asks about post-dose exposure, not trough assessment.

choices.label: Collect tacrolimus midway between scheduled doses
choices.rationale: A mid-interval concentration is not the intended predose trough and cannot be read against that target.
choices.temptation: Choose an apparently representative average time rather than the requested sampling window.
choices.reasonableWhen: A separately specified pharmacokinetic study asks for a mid-interval concentration.

nodes.explanation: The printed test name does not override the administration and collection record. A post-dose sample cannot be interpreted against the service's predose target. Repeat the intended collection before changing treatment on that basis.

reasoning.interpret: Determine that the specimen was collected after medication despite its label.
reasoning.apply: Choose the assessment that answers the intended exposure question before changing maintenance therapy.
reasoning.decidingObservation: Dose administration precedes collection, and the graft course is stable.
reasoning.counterfactual: If the intended protocol explicitly requested a post-dose pharmacokinetic specimen, collecting after the dose would answer that different question.
reasoning.consequence: A false high-trough interpretation can lead to unnecessary reduction and rejection risk.
reasoning.deletionTest: The administration-before-collection observation establishes the validity problem. Stable function and resolved symptoms distinguish it from earlier true toxicity. No exact post-dose interval or invented concentration is included.
reasoning.cueAttack: Replaced unrelated mycophenolate profiling and premature biopsy with three genuine tacrolimus collection windows. The sample was labelled trough but its actual administration/collection order must be checked, then the intended window selected. Every option names the same medicine and has the same laboratory wait.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three acquisition windows for the same drug-level assessment.
reasoning.difficultyReason: Prior true toxicity can anchor a dosing response; the learner must first detect the invalid labelled specimen and select the actual intended acquisition.
reasoning.sequenceReview: Prior feedback describes actual toxicity; the new record has different collection chronology and clinical response. It does not name the sampling error.

A second option attack found that unrelated drug profiling and biopsy were weak alternatives. Replaced them with same-drug post-dose and mid-interval sampling plans, then re-solved the actual acquisition error and intended trough window.
Replaced the repeated before word with the observed action in the phlebotomy note. The actual dose/draw order is preserved, so the learner must interpret chronology instead of copy a temporal word.

specs.presentation: {patientName}, a 55-year-old man with a kidney transplant, attends clinic for the founder to examine outside follow-up records after a changing neck swelling.

nodes.objective: Choose tissue evaluation when the lesion course and blood EBV trend diverge.
nodes.currentUpdate: The outside record shows that plasma EBV DNA fell across surveillance specimens. The left neck lymph node continued to enlarge, and abdominal imaging now shows additional nodes. The earlier aspirate contains blood and disrupted lymphoid cells; the report cannot classify the process. Creatinine remains at his baseline.
nodes.task: Which investigation best addresses {patientName}'s progressing nodal findings?

choices.label: Whole-body FDG PET/CT staging
choices.rationale: Distribution imaging is useful, but cannot supply the missing tissue classification of the progressing process.
choices.temptation: Choose the most comprehensive scan after a discordant trend.
choices.reasonableWhen: Tissue has already established the process and staging is the unresolved task.

choices.label: Representative lymph-node tissue biopsy
choices.rationale: The enlarging lesions remain unexplained despite the lower blood signal and the unclassifying aspirate.
choices.temptation: Separate blood response from tissue identity and choose a representative sample.
choices.reasonableWhen: A progressing lesion remains unclassified.

choices.label: Repeat plasma EBV quantitative testing
choices.rationale: Another blood trend cannot resolve the tissue question raised by the progressing nodes.
choices.temptation: Interpret falling EBV as an adequate surrogate for lesion behavior.
choices.reasonableWhen: The clinical task is viral surveillance after representative tissue has resolved the lesion question.

nodes.explanation: The blood EBV response does not classify enlarging tissue lesions. Obtain representative tissue with the transplant and hematology teams. This item selects the need for tissue, not excision versus core or a fresh/fixed allocation.

reasoning.interpret: Interpret the discordance between decreasing circulating EBV and increasing nodal disease.
reasoning.apply: Use the failed classification to choose representative tissue rather than another surrogate measurement.
reasoning.decidingObservation: The lesion progresses and the represented aspirate does not classify it.
reasoning.counterfactual: If representative tissue already established the process and extent were the remaining question, PET/CT would become the appropriate investigation.
reasoning.consequence: Accepting a blood response as a tissue diagnosis can delay identification of malignancy or a mimic.
reasoning.deletionTest: The lesion and blood trajectories are both essential. The actual aspirate findings establish what was sampled without implying that all needle techniques fail. Baseline graft function frames the prior medication response.
reasoning.cueAttack: Removed the task phrase nature of the nodal process that overlapped biopsy rationale. All choices are named investigations. The tissue option avoids full-classification and safety qualifiers that made earlier keys uniquely comprehensive.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three investigations during diagnostic characterization.
reasoning.difficultyReason: PET/CT is a credible next-stage competitor; blood response is a plausible anchoring error.
reasoning.sequenceReview: First node; no future pathology visible. The explanation does not name later treatment choices.

Removed prior immunosuppression reduction from the diagnostic-node history so the next initial PTLD treatment decision is not already completed or rehearsed.
Replaced ambiguous cervical wording with neck lymph node and removed generic header references to future tissue records; the progressing-lesion evidence is unchanged.

nodes.objective: Choose an initial immunosuppression direction after represented PTLD classification.
nodes.currentUpdate: The later tissue record establishes polymorphic B-cell PTLD, with EBV demonstrated in involved tissue. The staging record has no immediately threatening organ involvement. Graft function remains stable, and the recent graft assessment does not show rejection. The transplant and hematology teams are selecting the initial medication plan.
nodes.task: Which immunosuppression direction best fits {patientName}'s newly classified process?

choices.label: Increase the calcineurin-inhibitor exposure
choices.rationale: Escalating graft-directed suppression is not an initial way to address this represented lymphoproliferative complication.
choices.temptation: Treat every transplant complication as insufficient graft protection.
choices.reasonableWhen: The biopsy instead establishes acute rejection needing greater graft protection.

choices.label: Reduce the maintenance immunosuppressive burden
choices.rationale: Reduction is an initial component of PTLD care, weighed against graft risk with the treating teams.
choices.temptation: Integrate the tissue diagnosis with current graft stability.
choices.reasonableWhen: PTLD is established and the team judges reduction clinically appropriate.

choices.label: Continue the current immunosuppressive burden
choices.rationale: Avoiding any change protects the graft but does not address the modifiable immunosuppression contribution in the represented initial PTLD stage.
choices.temptation: Prioritize a stable graft over every competing host risk.
choices.reasonableWhen: Competing graft risk prevents reduction and a separately defined specialist plan is needed.

nodes.explanation: Established PTLD changes the balance of host and graft risks. A supervised reduction in maintenance immunosuppression is an initial component of care. The question does not specify a drug order, percentage, taper schedule or definitive oncology regimen.

reasoning.interpret: Use representative tissue to distinguish established PTLD from an EBV blood signal.
reasoning.apply: Balance the established process against the current stable graft when choosing an initial immunosuppression direction.
reasoning.decidingObservation: PTLD is tissue-classified, while the represented graft assessment does not show a competing rejection episode.
reasoning.counterfactual: If acute rejection posed an overriding graft threat, the reduction plan would need reconsideration by the treating teams; no universal schedule would follow.
reasoning.consequence: Failure to revisit maintenance burden can leave a contributing immunosuppressive state; indiscriminate withdrawal can harm the graft.
reasoning.deletionTest: Tissue classification establishes that this is a management task. Current graft findings and absence of immediately threatening disease delimit a reasonable initial direction without pretending to rank oncology regimens.
reasoning.cueAttack: All three options are immunosuppression directions with equal scope. Removed a key-only transplant/hematology coordination phrase by putting joint care in shared context.
reasoning.stageAudit: Three maintenance-immunosuppression strategies at initial PTLD management.
reasoning.difficultyReason: The credible error is preserving every maintenance drug because the graft is functioning, without balancing the established host complication.
reasoning.sequenceReview: Earlier feedback taught a diagnostic tissue boundary, not immunosuppression management. New classification earns a distinct treatment decision.
